articles.title: Identifying window trickle vents and recording their condition
articles.summary: An offline observational reference for identifying window trickle vents and recording their condition, with safe limits and follow-up notes.

visual.alt: Three labelled observation areas: Vent cover, Control, Window frame. A non-instructional schematic for recording visible condition, without depicting repairs.
visual.caption: Identify and record the concern without dismantling equipment.

sections.title: Recognise the component
paragraphs: A trickle vent is a small purpose-made opening, often near the top of a window frame. Designs differ, and not every narrow slot is a vent.
Use a visible maker marking or window paperwork to identify it; do not assume that one vent provides sufficient ventilation.
From a safe standing position, note missing covers, visible obstruction or damaged controls without removing any parts.
Record the room, window and symptom, such as a draught or suspected blockage. A photograph from floor level may help a specialist.
Check the window manufacturer's instructions before operating unfamiliar controls; never force a stuck fitting.
Persistent dampness or air-quality concerns need appropriate assessment rather than a guessed adjustment to one vent.

articles.title: Recognising washing-machine movement and foot-level concerns
articles.summary: An offline observational reference for recognising washing-machine movement and foot-level concerns, with safe limits and follow-up notes.

visual.alt: Three labelled observation areas: Floor, Machine, Feet. A non-instructional schematic for recording visible condition, without depicting repairs.
visual.caption: Identify and record the concern without dismantling equipment.

sections.title: Recognise the component
paragraphs: A machine that shifts or makes new knocking sounds during normal use may have an installation, loading or mechanical problem.
Noise alone does not identify a faulty foot; observe from a safe distance without touching an operating machine.
Record the model and when movement occurs during an ordinary cycle. Note any visible floor gap without tilting the machine.
Do not pull a connected appliance out of a recess or reach beneath it. Hidden hoses and electrical connections may be disturbed.
If movement is severe, a leak appears or electrical trouble is suspected, stop relying on the machine and arrange help.
Keep installation records available for an installer or technician to assess the floor, levelling and appliance condition.

articles.title: Checking a refrigerator door gasket for visible wear
articles.summary: An offline observational reference for checking a refrigerator door gasket for visible wear, with safe limits and follow-up notes.

visual.alt: Three labelled observation areas: Seal edge, Corners, Door contact. A non-instructional schematic for recording visible condition, without depicting repairs.
visual.caption: Identify and record the concern without dismantling equipment.

sections.title: Recognise the component
paragraphs: The gasket is the flexible strip around the door that meets the cabinet when it closes. Some designs are integrated into the door.
Look for obvious splits, folds or trapped packaging during ordinary opening, without pulling out or cutting the seal.
Record the model and which corner or edge looks affected. A door that does not close flush can have causes other than the gasket.
Visual appearance alone cannot confirm a safe storage temperature; follow appliance guidance and food-safety information separately.
Save a clear photograph and model details for manufacturer or service support, since replacement parts differ between models.
Avoid improvised adhesives or heating methods. Arrange assessment if the door repeatedly fails to close or cooling is in doubt.

articles.title: Making a household outside-tap identification record
articles.summary: An offline observational reference for making a household outside-tap identification record, with safe limits and follow-up notes.

visual.alt: Three labelled observation areas: Tap location, Wall entry, Service notes. A non-instructional schematic for recording visible condition, without depicting repairs.
visual.caption: Identify and record the concern without dismantling equipment.

sections.title: Recognise the component
paragraphs: Record each outdoor tap's location using a name another household member could recognise, such as rear garden wall.
Do not assume a visible tap has its own isolation valve or that a particular fitting is frost-resistant.
Note any readable maker details, visible dripping or missing handle from an accessible location.
Do not open panels, loosen connections or enter confined spaces to trace pipework; record uncertainty instead.
Keep manufacturer documents and a suitable plumbing contact with the household property records.
Never improvise pipe heating or use naked flames near frozen fittings. A location record does not replace winter maintenance advice.

articles.title: Recording moisture signs inside an under-sink cupboard
articles.summary: An offline observational reference for recording moisture signs inside an under-sink cupboard, with safe limits and follow-up notes.

visual.alt: Three labelled observation areas: Cabinet base, Back panel, Pipe area. A non-instructional schematic for recording visible condition, without depicting repairs.
visual.caption: Identify and record the concern without dismantling equipment.

sections.title: Recognise the component
paragraphs: An under-sink cupboard may contain pipes, stored chemicals and electrical equipment. Marks or swelling do not identify a specific leak.
Observe only through normal cupboard access without touching wet electrical equipment or dismantling connections.
Note where moisture appears and when it was first noticed. Record any change without repeatedly running water to recreate a leak.
Keep stored products closed and avoid shifting installed equipment to investigate inaccessible areas.
If water is actively escaping, damage is spreading or electricity may be affected, keep clear and seek suitable assistance.
A photograph and short timeline can help a plumber or property manager assess the concern; surface drying alone may not resolve it.

articles.title: Recognising wear in door threshold weatherstrips
articles.summary: An offline observational reference for recognising wear in door threshold weatherstrips, with safe limits and follow-up notes.

visual.alt: Three labelled observation areas: Threshold, Seal edge, Clearance. A non-instructional schematic for recording visible condition, without depicting repairs.
visual.caption: Identify and record the concern without dismantling equipment.

sections.title: Recognise the component
paragraphs: A weatherstrip may be a door sweep, threshold strip or frame seal. Different designs address draughts and water entry.
Observe torn, detached or catching strips during normal use, without removing anything from a fire-rated or unfamiliar door.
Record which entrance and edge are affected, and whether the symptom is scraping, water entry or failure to latch.
Do not wedge open a shared fire door or change hardware that may affect accessibility or safe closure.
Consult the door maker or property manager before selecting a replacement part; similar-looking seals may differ.
Arrange appropriate help if the door does not latch, is fire-rated, or shows persistent water damage.

articles.title: Observing a bathroom extractor grille without opening the fan
articles.summary: An offline observational reference for observing a bathroom extractor grille without opening the fan, with safe limits and follow-up notes.

visual.alt: Three labelled observation areas: Grille face, Visible dust, Service notes. A non-instructional schematic for recording visible condition, without depicting repairs.
visual.caption: Identify and record the concern without dismantling equipment.

sections.title: Recognise the component
paragraphs: An extractor grille is the visible cover of a fan or duct opening. Its construction varies by model.
From floor level note obvious damage or staining; never touch a running fan or remove covers to inspect internal parts.
Record whether the concern is noise, visible dust or poor apparent ventilation. Appearance cannot confirm airflow performance.
Keep the room and model details from existing paperwork, avoiding unnecessary photographs of personal belongings.
Consult the manufacturer's instructions to identify authorised maintenance and suitable servicing arrangements.
High access, electrical concerns or persistent dampness warrant professional assessment; do not block the opening.

articles.title: Building a household appliance model-label index
articles.summary: An offline observational reference for building a household appliance model-label index, with safe limits and follow-up notes.

visual.alt: Three labelled observation areas: Appliance, Model ID, Manual. A non-instructional schematic for recording visible condition, without depicting repairs.
visual.caption: Identify and record the concern without dismantling equipment.

sections.title: Recognise the component
paragraphs: Record each major appliance's room, manufacturer and exact model when readily available from paperwork or a visible label.
Similar-looking products may require different parts, so do not infer a model number from appearance alone.
Group entries by room and save the location of an offline or paper manual. Avoid putting private account details into a shared index.
Do not pull heavy connected appliances forward or open covers just to find a label; mark uncertain details unconfirmed.
Update the index after equipment is replaced, moved or sold, with a simple date for each change.
Check that saved manuals open without a connection. Identification records support servicing but do not authorise hazardous repair.
